title: The biggest move was ranked 116th
headline: The biggest dollar move ranked 116th by percent.
dek: The board's 7-day list ranks moves by percent. Across the 126 cards that have made it since Oct 13, the largest dollar move is a Mew from the 30th Celebration set that fell about $1,043, from $5,322 to $4,278.49 (−19.6%), on the Oct 26 list: 116th of 126 by percent. And 74% of all the dollars moved came from 36 cards, those whose biggest move ended at $100 or more. We rank by percent because it compares a $25 card with a $500 one fairly; it also means the list can't show where the dollars moved. Every move is unconfirmed.
why_now: Every File this fall has ranked moves the way the board does, by percent, so the cheap cards fill the page. This is the week to say what that choice hides, because the card that moved the most dollars in six weeks was never the headline.
risk: One row is not a finding. The Mew appears once, on one list, as a 19.6% move on a $5,000 card, and no sale was checked behind it, so it may be one thin sale's reading rather than a market move. Dollars are the wrong unit for most questions: $1,043 on a $5,300 card is a smaller move than $122 on a $200 card, and the board can't tell which matters to you. "Each card's largest move" is our choice of how to count a card that appears on many lists. Start-of-week prices are worked back from the listed price and its rounded change. This is not a read on whether these prices are high or low.
what_to_watch: Whether a card worth $100 or more makes the 7-day list again with a large dollar move and a modest percent, and whether a sale is checked behind it when it does. And an idea, not built: a second list of the biggest moves in dollars, beside the one in percent, for cards worth $100 or more.
source: TCGplayer market prices via tcgcsv.com, from the board's published 7-day lists, Oct 13 to Nov 14, 2026 (33 mornings, 330 rows, 126 cards)

foot: Market price: TCGplayer's average of recent completed sales of the same card, condition and printing (help.tcgplayer.com). The counts: the board's own published 7-day lists, Oct 13 to Nov 14, 2026, 33 mornings (git history of data/movers.json), 330 rows, 126 distinct cards. For each card, its largest 7-day move in dollars (listed price minus the start-of-week price worked back from the listed price and its rounded change) and its largest in percent, each over every list it appeared on. Cards were ranked on each unit separately: the Mew ranks 1st by dollars and 116th by percent. Top ten by dollars and top ten by percent share 3 cards (Pikachu ex 107, Umbreon ex 110 and Pikachu DP16). Summing each card's largest dollar move gives $5,032; 73.7% of it ($3,710) comes from the 36 cards whose largest-dollar move ended at $100 or more. The table: four cards at the row named in each note; start-of-week prices are worked back, so within a dollar. The list: up to 10 Pokémon cards worth $20 or more that moved 5% or more in a week, ranked by percent; with no checked sales, a move shows only if it's 60% or less, the lowest listing moved the same way by at least a quarter as much, the price changed in the last 2 days, and the card trades. Unconfirmed: no sale checked by Mission Control's Sale Integrity Layer in that window. Not advice.
